video.title: Psychology of Charisma: How To Actually Make People Like You

protocol.status: second independent labeler (B), for the noise floor
protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output.
protocol.times_from: Whisper small transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Cold-open thesis: standard charisma advice treats it as a signal you transmit, but charisma is what people feel about themselves around you. Can end on that line or on the 'instrument nobody is listening to' kicker.

The Toronto study splits charisma into influence and affability; all popular advice trains influence, which without affability reads as intensity. Can open on 'Let's start by naming the thing properly'.

Reis and Shaver's perceived partner responsiveness (understanding, validation, caring): nothing on the list is about you, so you create the conditions for liking. Can open on the question 'what is affability made of?'.
Fiske's warmth vs competence: warmth is judged first because the ancestral question was 'are you going to hurt me?', so brightness gets you looked at and warmth draws people in.

Tight, punchy point: the harder you try to be liked the worse you get, because self-monitoring takes attention off the other person. 'You are not failing because you are boring. You are failing because you are busy.'
Boothby's liking-gap study: people underestimate how much they're liked because they grade their own performance. Can end on the finding or run on through 'the full shape of the trap'.
Follow-up questions predict being liked (speed-dating data); 'two people taking turns waiting' vs actually staying on what they said. Drop the bare 'Law 1.' at the start.
Beautiful mess effect: we read our own vulnerability as weakness and others' as courage, so one honest sentence first makes it safe for the other person. Complete and quotable.

Moreland and Beach's lecture-hall study: the women who were simply present more often were liked more, without saying a word, so liking is built by frequency. Can end at 'built by frequency' or after the practical tips.

also_ok.why: Longer version that runs through the training argument (school, interviews, social media teach you to audition) into 'busy, not boring'. Good, but 'get this wrong' leans on the prior section.
'Just be confident' fails because confidence is an output, not an input; Antonakis showed charisma behaviours can be trained. Works as a short 25s cut or with the study.
Practical law with a strong closing line ('Competence introduced first is judged; after warmth, admired'). Opens with 'Remember what Fiske found', a light callback.
Genuine specific compliments land better and feel less awkward than people predict (Zhao and Epley); 'nice shirt is noise'. Ends before 'Law 4' inside the same sentence.
Capitalization research: how you respond to good news matters as much as support in bad times; expand the moment instead of 'congrats' and a change of subject.
Closing monologue: charisma becomes a by-product of where your attention goes; Simone Weil on attention as generosity. It can start at either 805 or 836; the 805 start is inside the band.

negatives.why: Channel intro ('Welcome back to PsychToons... six laws... backed by real research'): a promise, not content.
Comment prompt that lists all six laws by name; sounds like a summary but only works if you saw them.
Quotable 'people already like you more than you think' line, but it's an 11s callback to the liking gap and the outro's lead-in.
